dialogue.text: [serious, engaging] But governments that owe too much have an easy way out: they make their money worth less. In 1933, America ordered its citizens to hand in their gold at twenty dollars and sixty-seven cents an ounce, then less than a year later set the price at thirty-five. The government made sixty-nine percent, and the people who handed it in made nothing.
[serious, engaging] So the real risk isn't that your money disappears overnight. It's that it buys a little less every year, and nobody sends you a letter about it.
[serious, engaging] So far, we've followed the money down. Now let's see where it lands, because this is where the world gets a new boss.

[serious, engaging] When everything breaks, stock prices stop mattering. A country survives on what it can't print: food, energy, factories, an army, and whether the rest of the world still trusts its money.

[serious, engaging] Europe buys more than half of its energy from abroad, so its factories and its heating bills get hit first. Japan and the Gulf states have the same weak spot: they import their energy or their food.

[serious, engaging] China is the real contender. It makes almost a third of everything manufactured on Earth, it has stockpiled about half the world's wheat, and its central bank keeps buying gold. But our captain is still at anchor, because China's customers are broke, and much of its oil comes through the Strait of Hormuz.

[serious, engaging] And then there's America, where the first domino fell. It pumps more oil than any country in history, grows far more grain than it eats, has an ocean on each side and the strongest military on Earth.
